title: DSA - Quick Sort - Fixing It
description:
## The Problem
Your quicksort picks the last element as pivot. What happens with an already sorted array?

```
[1, 2, 3, 4, 5]  pivot = 5
Partition: everything goes left, nothing goes right
[1, 2, 3, 4] [5] []

[1, 2, 3, 4]  pivot = 4
[1, 2, 3] [4] []

[1, 2, 3]  pivot = 3
...
```

Every partition only removes ONE element. That's n partitions of n elements = **O(n²)**. The worst case.

## The Fix: Random Pivot
Instead of always picking the last element, pick a random one and swap it to the end before partitioning:

```cpp
int random_index = low + (rand() % (high - low + 1));
std::swap(arr[random_index], arr[high]);
// now partition as normal
```

This makes the worst case astronomically unlikely. Average stays O(n log n).
### rand() in C++
`rand()` returns a random integer. To get a number in a range:
```cpp
#include <cstdlib>

// random number between low and high (inclusive)
int random_index = low + (rand() % (high - low + 1));
```

`%` gives the remainder, which limits the range. Adding `low` shifts it to start at `low`.

---
## Assignment:
Copy your quicksort from the previous lesson and modify the `partition` function to pick a random pivot instead of always using the last element.

Add `#include <cstdlib>` for `rand()`.

### Steps:
- [ ] At the start of `partition`, generate a random index between `low` and `high`
- [ ] Swap `arr[random_index]` with `arr[high]`
- [ ] Continue with the same partition logic as before
hint: Just add two lines at the start of partition: generate random index, swap with arr[high]. Everything else stays the same.
